name: Carlos Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Tell me how a normal day on the power lines goes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an electricity company line crew, often after a fault has already sent three different reports to dispatch. I draw the likely section on a tablet, then we go to the pole and test before anyone touches the wire. My two-year diploma helps with the network drawing, but a younger worker spotting a cracked insulator can save me a lot of time. At home my partner and I juggle two children’s school days and a mortgage, so I value the higher pay this lead role brings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI is already handy for sorting fault reports, even if the big claims fall flat. I use it every day to group repeated outage notes, then the crew checks the actual line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings cover more than six months and my lead pay is good, so the mortgage is not hanging on a new software feature. I mainly worry about people treating a suggested fault location as a confirmed one. An AI outage map can point at a street; my line crew still has to find the broken wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current lead rota and continue checking AI grouped reports against the crew’s site readings. During the first year I would teach our newest apprentice to mark an unconfirmed fault clearly on the tablet before dispatch sends another crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, perhaps a bit amused by the grand talk. A small sorting improvement helps us find the right street, and I still get to do the work I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which report do you distrust most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer may report sparks on the next street when the fault is at the transformer behind it. I make the crew confirm the section on site before marking the outage resolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think about your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner likes that our higher lead wage and savings cover the mortgage and school costs. We still plan expenses together, but one bad AI summary would not change our household budget.

say: **Daily** AI sorting helps group outage reports, while the crew confirms each fault.
I would **label** suggested fault locations as unconfirmed until field readings agree.
think: **Strong** savings and higher lead pay make modest AI change safe for our mortgage.
A **suggested** location can misdirect the next crew if treated as certain.
do: **Keep** lead rota and compare grouped reports with site readings.
**Teach** newest apprentice to mark unconfirmed tablet locations clearly.
feel: **Calm** about income and pleased with a useful sorting tool.
S0.quote: An AI outage map can point at a street; my line crew still has to find the broken wire.
fieldNote: He **already** uses AI daily but separates a suggested map from field proof.
**Higher** pay and more than six months of savings support household calm.

steps.text: Keep lead rota and check AI grouped reports against site readings
Teach apprentice to mark unconfirmed fault locations on tablet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that stronger AI could sort tickets and buy parts faster, and I would try the new fault triage tool. I would also ask our union group to insist that workers can correct its maps and see how errors are fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The desk side could lose jobs first, while physical line repair stays busy. My own higher wage is probably safe for now, though I do not want apprentices hired in smaller numbers because a screen looks efficient. A wrong AI fault map becomes a safety problem when the next line crew cannot see the correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the triage tool beside our usual outage board for six weeks and record every wrong section or missed pole. In the first year I would take the log to our union technology group and request a shared correction record for dispatch and field crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious and mostly calm about my own work. I would be less settled if an apprentice had no way to learn the faults the tool gets wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the shared correction record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool’s suggested section, the measured fault, the crew correction and the date someone changed the map. I want the next shift to see the fix, not repeat the same detour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the union into a tool you want to use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker should be able to report a bad map without being blamed for slowing a target. Our union group can insist the correction trail stays visible to every crew.

say: I would **test** AI fault triage beside the outage board for six weeks.
Our **union** group should secure a shared correction trail for field errors.
think: **Desk** work may shrink before line repair, while my higher wage looks secure for now.
**Fewer** apprentice openings would weaken the trade even if my own job holds.
do: **Test** triage suggestions against measured faults for six weeks.
**Bring** wrong-section records to union technology group.
**Request** visible correction trail for dispatch and field crews.
feel: **Curious** and mostly calm about work, with concern for apprentices.
S1.quote: A wrong AI fault map becomes a safety problem when the next line crew cannot see the correction.
fieldNote: He is an **early** tool user who also wants shared accountability for error reports.
His **concern** for apprentice hiring does not become an invented immediate threat to his own income.

steps.text: Test AI fault triage against measured line faults for six weeks
Bring triage error log to union technology group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI by 2028 might draw nearly every fault plan, and capable robots around 2031 might act on them. I would join paid line robot trials early, with the crew able to stop a machine and share its failure log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am excited to learn, but three years is short for the field wage to change. We have over six months saved and plenty of nearby line jobs, yet a sharp cut in paid callouts would still alter what we can afford for the children. A robot can recover from a bad test in the yard; a power line crew owns the dark street afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply this year for a paid robot trial shift and ask the union technology group for a common failure log. In the first year after 2028 I would learn the robot stop controls during paid trials, then put two hundred from each actual monthly pay packet into additional savings while we watch callout hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the speed, even with options. I want my crew in the trial room because I know how fast a small line error becomes a whole street without power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop the robot for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop it if the proposed isolation point did not match our measured line or if its grip loaded a damaged crossarm. The written trial rule must let the crew lead halt it without losing pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the company offers only unpaid testing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my lead shifts and let the union group push for paid trials. The family has savings, but testing the company’s equipment is work, not my private hobby.

say: I would **join** paid robot trials before machines work live lines around 2031.
**Crews** need stop controls and a shared failure log as thinking AI arrives in 2028.
think: **Callout** income could shrink quickly, despite strong savings and many nearby jobs.
**Children** and mortgage make a sharp loss of higher pay matter.
do: **Apply** for paid robot trial shift this year.
**Learn** robot stop controls on paid trials after 2028.
**Save** two hundred extra from each actual monthly pay packet after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about the fast schedule but ready to test with worker controls.
S2.quote: A robot can recover from a bad test in the yard; a power line crew owns the dark street afterward.
fieldNote: He is **eager** to test machines, while pay and crew stop authority remain conditions.
**New** savings are drawn from future pay packets, rather than relabelling an existing reserve.

steps.text: Learn robot stop controls on paid trials after 2028
Ask union technology group for shared robot failure log
Save two hundred extra from each monthly pay packet after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the years to 2031 for thinking AI and 2034 for capable robots give us enough time to design a paid line robot examiner job. I would want crews, the company and apprentices to test what the machine does on ordinary faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be well placed to examine robot repairs with my diploma and crew lead experience. A real job offer matters more than a title, but with our savings and many nearby employers I can take time to compare pay and field duties. A line robot examiner should find the broken crossarm before signing the machine’s repair safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year to publish the robot examiner job description, pay and course dates. If it funds field training and posts a role at least matching my lead wage, I would enroll before 2031 and apply in the first year after thinking AI arrives; otherwise I would keep my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and calm about my own income. The extra years make it possible to learn from real faults before I choose a different badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What field test would you want in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a broken crossarm and a wrong meter reading in the same exercise. The examiner must find both before signing a machine repair safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if another firm posts a better role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the written wage, location and field authority with our company’s offer. Plenty of nearby jobs give choices, but I would not leave my crew on a rumour.

say: A **longer** runway could create a paid field examiner role before line robots arrive around 2034.
**Apprentices** and crews should test ordinary faults, not only demonstrations.
think: My **diploma** and lead work suit examination if an actual comparable offer appears.
**Strong** savings and nearby employers let me compare real pay and field authority.
do: **Request** written examiner duties, salary and course dates this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if company funds field course and posts matching-pay role.
**Apply** after 2031 only if posted examiner role matches current lead wage.
feel: **Interested** and calm about my own income while real job terms can be compared.
S3.quote: A line robot examiner should find the broken crossarm before signing the machine’s repair safe.
fieldNote: His **interest** in a new role rests on funded field training and an actual comparable opening.
**Local** options and savings give time to compare offers, without inventing an automatic promotion.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if funded field course and matching-pay role posted
Apply after 2031 if posted examiner role matches lead wage
Keep power line crew if suitable examiner offer is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices that a decade before thinking AI and another three years before capable robots is time to learn both pole work and machine checks. I would like the company and union to create paid practice days on real faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three, I might be ready to spend more days teaching and fewer nights on storm repairs, if the mortgage and family timetable allow. I would not call it retirement, and I do not know what vacancies will exist then. A paid apprentice day should end with a measured power line, not just a clever AI map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would bring a paid practice-day proposal to the union training committee and keep leading field shifts. If the company later posts a paid apprentice lead role with salary that covers our mortgage, I would apply in the first year after 2036 and move only after a firm offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about a long runway. I can teach a younger worker to challenge an AI map while still earning from the repair crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen on a practice day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice would compare the AI fault map with field measurements, then explain any wrong section to the crew. I would make the lesson part of paid time, not an extra unpaid evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take less pay to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might consider it once my partner and I know the remaining mortgage and the actual hours. Today I would keep the higher lead wage rather than promise a future cut.

say: A **decade** permits paid practice days that join field measurements with AI maps.
I would **keep** apprentices learning real line faults before robots arrive around 2039.
think: **Teaching** could suit later family life if actual hours and mortgage balance permit.
I do **not** treat a teaching move as retirement or a guaranteed vacancy.
do: **Bring** paid practice-day proposal to union training committee this year.
**Keep** leading field repairs while apprentice plan develops.
**Apply** after 2036 if posted apprentice lead role covers mortgage.
feel: **Calm** with years to teach, compare offers and keep earning.
S4.quote: A paid apprentice day should end with a measured power line, not just a clever AI map.
fieldNote: He **sees** teaching as a paid job option while maintaining field income.
The **union** proposal is collective work; later movement depends on a posted salary and family budget.

steps.text: Bring paid practice-day proposal to union training committee
Keep leading power line repairs while apprentice plan develops
Apply after 2036 if posted apprentice lead role covers mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could reach ordinary repairs around 2031 before anyone knows what happens to callout pay. Paid trials, a crew stop rule and shared failure logs would help. I will learn the robot controls, but I want a line crew beside the machine when the first wet pole goes wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a younger worker will still get to find faults instead of only watching a screen. My diploma helped, but the crew taught me to look twice before declaring a street safe. A robot should make that lesson more urgent, not erase it.

headlineQuote: I will learn the robot controls, but I want a line crew beside the machine when the first wet pole goes wrong.
portrait: **Carlos** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma who uses AI daily to sort outage reports.
His **higher** wage and more than six months of savings support a partner, two school-age children and mortgage.
He **volunteers** for paid line robot trials and uses union groups to demand visible corrections, failure logs and crew stop rules.
With **more** time he considers funded field examination or paid apprentice teaching, subject to real posts and adequate salary.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring capable line robots into ordinary repairs around 2031 before callout pay and stop rules are clear.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** trials, crew stop authority and shared failure logs would let workers test machines while guarding field safety.
